title: Hardware Additions
summary: Hardware additions are the introduction of physical computing or networking devices into an environment to create access that did not exist before. The category covers more than a USB stick carrying files: it includes single board computers hidden behind a desk, rogue wireless access points, network taps, inline devices that rewrite traffic, keystroke injectors that present themselves as keyboards, and expansion cards that read memory directly. Because the device is physically present, it can create its own outbound channel, for example a mobile data link, and it can also be placed inline to observe or alter traffic between two legitimate systems. Telemetry is often network side: an unknown device requesting an address, a new physical port coming up on a switch, an unexpected wireless network with a similar name, or a workstation suddenly talking to a gateway that nobody documented. Physical and asset records matter just as much, since the strongest evidence is usually the difference between what is plugged in and what the inventory says should be there.

beginner.definition: This means someone puts a new piece of hardware into your network or computer. It could be a tiny computer, a hidden wireless box or a device that sits between two cables. The device gives the attacker a way in or a way to watch. The attacker usually needs physical access for only a short time.
beginner.whyItMatters: One short visit can create access that lasts for months. A rogue wireless box lets an attacker connect from a car park, well away from your building. An inline device can watch or change traffic without any software on your computers. If you only monitor software, you may never see the new device sitting in the room.
howItWorks: The attacker gets brief physical access, as a visitor, a cleaner or a contractor.
They plug a small device into a network socket, a computer port or between two existing cables.
The device powers up and may connect to the internet through its own mobile data link.
It can offer a hidden wireless network, copy traffic, or act as a keyboard that types commands.
On the network it may request an address and appear as an ordinary new machine.
The attacker then uses this foothold remotely, and the device may stay in place for a long time.
beginner.example: Picture a shared flat where everyone trusts the front door lock. A visitor arrives, fits a spare key box under the stairs, and leaves twenty minutes later. The flat looks exactly the same. From then on, anyone who knows the code can walk in while the residents are out. Nobody broke anything, and the lock was never picked.
takeaways: Physical access for a few minutes can create remote access for months.
Know what should be connected, and check network ports and wireless networks for anything else.
Lock network cabinets and unused wall sockets, and escort visitors in sensitive areas.

objectives: Describe types of hardware that can be added to gain access, such as rogue access points and inline taps.
Explain the difference between hardware additions and copying files with removable storage.
Identify network and asset evidence that reveals an unauthorised device.
Describe why physical access control is a security control and not only a facilities matter.
Explain how removable-media techniques differ from devices that add new capability to a system.
